Am I certain? Doc, I am... I mean, absolutely, one hundred percent certain. You don't just imagine this kind of thing. Like I was saying, it all started literally the week after that county safety award banquet. Before that, everything was fine, I was just a regular guy doing his job, keeping the buses on the road. Like, if I write 'monitor rear suspension for future wear,' they try to spin it in the system to say I 'ignored an active hazard.' It's insane. It's a deliberate twisting of my words. 

And then I go to my supervisor, I literally put the emails right on his desk. I printed them out, I highlighted the discrepancies, I showed him the timestamps, everything. I laid out the whole pattern. And he just sighs, leans back in his chair, and gives me this canned corporate line. 'Oh, it's just a normal review, everyone goes through it, don't worry about it.' But I know everyone doesn't go through it! I've been working there since I was twenty-two, right out of high school basically, and nobody gets grilled like this unless management is trying to build a paper trail to fire them. I can tell, I can just feel it in the room, the way the dispatchers stop talking when I walk in... there is absolutely a coordinated effort to discredit me. Well, if you really want to pin down a timeline, it’s been about a year. Yeah, right around a year now. It all started—and I remember this clearly because of the timing—right after I got recognized for the county safety initiative. 

See, the county transit authority does this thing every spring, usually around April, where they roll out these new safety protocols and they recognize staff who go above and beyond. And last year, they handed me this certificate—it’s just a piece of paper, really, printed on that thick cardstock with the county seal stamped in the corner—because I caught a systemic issue with the pneumatic doors on the 40-foot hybrid buses. It was a huge deal. I mean, if those doors fail while the bus is in motion, you’re looking at a massive liability, potential passenger injury, a PR nightmare for the county. I documented the whole thing, submitted a 15-page report with photographs and schematics, and they had to pull twelve buses off the line to fix the actuators. 

They gave me a plaque at the monthly all-hands meeting. The director shook my hand. And I thought, you know, I thought it was a good thing. I thought I was doing my job and protecting the public. But that’s exactly when the temperature in the garage changed. That’s when the plotting started. 

Because, think about it, by finding that flaw, I made the maintenance guys look bad. I made Mike, the lead mechanic, look incompetent because his team missed it during their routine checks. And Dave in scheduling had to scramble to cover the routes for those twelve buses, which messed up his whole board for a month. So instead of saying, 'Hey, good catch, you saved us a lawsuit,' they started looking at me like I was the enemy. 

It started small. Like, right after the ceremony, maybe a week later, I noticed my inspection logs were being moved. Not thrown away, just... shifted on my desk. Just enough to let me know someone had been in my workspace. Then it escalated to the whispers in the breakroom, the sudden silence when I walked into the dispatch office. And it’s just been building and building for twelve months straight. Every single day for a year, I’ve had to watch my back, double-check my own locks on my tool chest, make copies of every single form I submit, because I know—I know for a fact—they are just waiting for me to slip up so they can get me fired and go back to running things their sloppy, dangerous way. So, yeah, a year. A whole year of this.

Completely standard stuff, I've filled out hundreds of them. Two days later, they pull me into this little glass office—the one by the vending machines where everyone in the breakroom can see you—and they start grilling me on why the parts requisition took an extra twelve dollars. Twelve dollars! They were asking these incredibly pointed budget questions, looking at me over their clipboards like I'm running some kind of black market parts ring out of the garage, just really trying to make me look crooked. \n\nAnd it's not just the money, they take my actual inspection notes, the ones I write meticulously, and they completely twist the wording around. Like, if I write 'monitor rear suspension for future wear,' they try to spin it in the system to say I 'ignored an active hazard.' It's insane. It's a deliberate twisting of my words. \n\nAnd then I go to my supervisor, I literally put the emails right on his desk. I printed them out, I highlighted the discrepancies, I showed him the timestamps, everything. I laid out the whole pattern. And he just sighs, leans back in his chair, and gives me this canned corporate line. 'Oh, it's just a normal review, everyone goes through it, don't worry about it.' But I know everyone doesn't go through it! I've been working there since I was twenty-two, right out of high school basically, and nobody gets grilled like this unless management is trying to build a paper trail to fire them. I can tell, I can just feel it in the room, the way the dispatchers stop talking when I walk in... there is absolutely a coordinated effort to discredit me. They want to ruin my reputation so they can push me out, and I am absolutely certain of it. You'd have to be blind not to see the pieces moving.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: Voices? Like... like people who aren't there? No, doc, no. I know why you're asking that, I mean, you're a psychiatrist, you have to run down the checklist, right? Make sure I'm not, you know, totally losing my grip or hallucinating. But no, absolutely not. The things I'm hearing... the conversations I'm talking about, they are coming from actual, physical people standing right there in the depot. It's not in my head. \n\nLike, okay, our breakroom at the garage has these super thin drywall partitions—the cheap kind they threw up back in the nineties when they expanded the dispatch center—and you can hear practically everything through them. So when I say I hear them talking, I don't mean some spooky disembodied voices or whatever. I mean I can literally hear Dave from scheduling or Mike, the lead mechanic, standing by the coffee maker—the big industrial one that always leaks a little water on the linoleum—and they are actually whispering about my reports. I hear real words from real people. \n\nActually, my hearing is perfect. I had to do a full DOT physical and an audiogram when I got promoted to inspector, and I scored top marks on the high-frequency tones. So maybe that's the problem, really. They think they're keeping their voices down, they think they're being so slick whispering behind the vending machines, but I can hear the actual sound of them trying to set me up. But voices when no one is there? No, never. If I hear someone talking, you better believe there's a guy in a county uniform standing right there doing the talking.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone told you that your speech is hard to follow or that your thoughts seem jumbled?\n\nPatient: Hard to follow? Jumbled? No, no, definitely not. I mean, if anything, I’m the one who has to constantly clarify things for everyone else. You know how it is in county government, right? You get these memos that are just total word salad, all this bureaucratic jargon—'synergizing maintenance protocols' and 'optimizing operational bandwidth.' It’s nonsense. I'm the guy who actually reads the manual, understands the code, and communicates it clearly. \n\nI mean, look, when I write an inspection report, it is crystal clear. I use bullet points, I reference the exact section of the safety manual—like Section 4, Paragraph B, regarding hydraulic fluid viscosity—I lay it all out logically. My thoughts are perfectly organized. I have to be organized to do my job, to keep track of all the different buses, the maintenance schedules, the parts inventory. If my thoughts were jumbled, I’d be approving vehicles with faulty steering columns or missing brake pads, and I don't do that. I catch the things other people miss because my mind works in a very systematic, logical way. \n\nNo one has ever told me I'm hard to follow. Well, except maybe my supervisor, but that's only when I'm trying to explain the conspiracy to him, and he just doesn't want to hear it. He'll say, 'Slow down, you're jumping all over the place,' but I'm not jumping all over the place, I'm just trying to connect the dots for him! I'm trying to show him how the email from Dave on Tuesday connects to the missing requisition form on Thursday, and how that ties into the way Mike was looking at me in the breakroom on Friday. It's all connected, and I can explain it perfectly, step-by-step, but they just... they pretend it's confusing because they don't want to admit what's really going on. But my actual speech? My thoughts? No, they're sharp. They have to be. If I wasn't thinking clearly, they would have gotten rid of me by now. I have to stay ten steps ahead of them just to keep my job.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe anyone outside of your workplace is also trying to harm or plot against you?\n\nPatient: Outside of work? No, no, I don't think so. I mean, why would they? My whole life, my whole routine, it really revolves around the depot. I get up, I go to the garage, I do my inspections, I come home. I don't really have a lot of hobbies or, you know, a huge social circle where people would even care enough to plot against me. I mean, I go to the grocery store—the one on 4th Street, usually on Sunday mornings when it's quiet—and nobody there is looking at me weird or following me down the cereal aisle or anything. I live in this little apartment complex, just a bunch of people keeping to themselves. Nobody is, like, tapping my phone lines or watching my apartment. I mean, I check, obviously. But it's always just the usual cars—the blue Honda, the rusty pickup truck. \n\nSo, no, the problem is entirely contained at the workplace. That's the arena. That's where the threat is. They want my job, they want to discredit my inspections, and they want me gone from the county transit authority. They don't care what I do on my own time, as long as I'm not in that garage finding their mistakes. They just want to push me out of the picture at work. So, yeah, outside of work, I feel totally fine. I can actually relax a little bit when I'm at home, you know? At least until Sunday night, when I have to start thinking about going back into that snake pit on Monday morning.\n\nDoctor: How long have you believed your coworkers were plotting against you?\n\nPatient: Well, if you really want to pin down a timeline, it’s been about a year. Yeah, right around a year now. It all started—and I remember this clearly because of the timing—right after I got recognized for the county safety initiative. \n\nSee, the county transit authority does this thing every spring, usually around April, where they roll out these new safety protocols and they recognize staff who go above and beyond. And last year, they handed me this certificate—it’s just a piece of paper, really, printed on that thick cardstock with the county seal stamped in the corner—because I caught a systemic issue with the pneumatic doors on the 40-foot hybrid buses. It was a huge deal. I mean, if those doors fail while the bus is in motion, you’re looking at a massive liability, potential passenger injury, a PR nightmare for the county. I documented the whole thing, submitted a 15-page report with photographs and schematics, and they had to pull twelve buses off the line to fix the actuators. \n\nThey gave me a plaque at the monthly all-hands meeting. The director shook my hand. And I thought, you know, I thought it was a good thing. I thought I was doing my job and protecting the public. But that’s exactly when the temperature in the garage changed. That’s when the plotting started. \n\nBecause, think about it, by finding that flaw, I made the maintenance guys look bad. I made Mike, the lead mechanic, look incompetent because his team missed it during their routine checks. And last year, they handed me this certificate—it’s just a piece of paper, really, printed on that thick cardstock with the county seal stamped in the corner—because I caught a systemic issue with the pneumatic doors on the 40-foot hybrid buses. It was a huge deal. I mean, if those doors fail while the bus is in motion, you’re looking at a massive liability, potential passenger injury, a PR nightmare for the county. I documented the whole thing, submitted a 15-page report with photographs and schematics, and they had to pull twelve buses off the line to fix the actuators. \n\nThey gave me a plaque at the monthly all-hands meeting. The director shook my hand. And I thought, you know, I thought it was a good thing. I thought I was doing my job and protecting the public. But that’s exactly when the temperature in the garage changed. That’s when the plotting started. \n\nBecause, think about it, by finding that flaw, I made the maintenance guys look bad. I made Mike, the lead mechanic, look incompetent because his team missed it during their routine checks. And Dave in scheduling had to scramble to cover the routes for those twelve buses, which messed up his whole board for a month. So instead of saying, 'Hey, good catch, you saved us a lawsuit,' they started looking at me like I was the enemy. \n\nIt started small. Like, right after the ceremony, maybe a week later, I noticed my inspection logs were being moved. Not thrown away, just... shifted on my desk. Just enough to let me know someone had been in my workspace. Then it escalated to the whispers in the breakroom, the sudden silence when I walked into the dispatch office. And it’s just been building and building for twelve months straight. Every single day for a year, I’ve had to watch my back, double-check my own locks on my tool chest, make copies of every single form I submit, because I know—I know for a fact—they are just waiting for me to slip up so they can get me fired and go back to running things their sloppy, dangerous way. So, yeah, a year. A whole year of this.\n\nDoctor: Apart from your coworkers plotting against you, have you had any other beliefs that other people say are strange or not true?\n\nPatient: Other beliefs? No. No, definitely not. I mean, I'm a very grounded guy. The only thing people say is \"not true\" or \"strange\" is... well, it's exactly what I'm here for. It's the situation at work. \n\nBecause, look, I’m here because ever since that county safety award—the one I was just telling you about with the pneumatic doors—certain people at work have been literally twisting my inspection reports. I’ll write a physical report, right? I'll note that a tie rod is showing early signs of fatigue, just standard preventative maintenance. I'll cite the manual. But then it goes up the chain, and suddenly it's being framed like I'm flagging perfectly good vehicles just to cause trouble and slow down the routes. \n\nAnd then come the budget questions. Oh, man, the budget questions. Out of nowhere, I've got people from procurement and administration asking me these incredibly pointed budget questions, demanding I justify the cost of the replacement parts I'm recommending.\n\nDoctor: If your supervisor showed you clear proof that the reviews and questions were routine and not directed at you, would you accept that?\n\nPatient: Proof? What kind of proof could he possibly show me? Look, my supervisor, he’s—well, he’s part of the whole system, isn't he? He’s the one who sits me down and tells me, \"Oh, it's just a normal review, everyone goes through this, it's standard operating procedure.\" Standard operating procedure. That's the phrase he uses, like it’s some kind of magic wand that makes the truth disappear. \n\nBut I'm the one on the ground. I'm the one who sees the actual paperwork before it gets, you know, sanitized or whatever they do to it upstairs. I see how they take my reports—reports that are meticulously detailed, by the way, based on the manufacturer's own safety tolerances—and they twist them. They twist the narrative so it looks like I'm the problem. They make it seem like I'm just flagging things to be difficult or to drain the budget. And then they hit me with those budget questions. \"Why are you recommending this part? Do you know how much this costs the county?\" Like they’re trying to make me look crooked, like I'm getting kickbacks from the parts supplier or something ridiculous like that. \n\nSo if my supervisor brings me a spreadsheet or an email chain and says, \"See? Even when he sits there with a straight face and tells me it's normal, I can tell. I can read between the lines. I see the patterns. There is a coordinated effort to discredit me, to make me look like a liability so they can push me out and go back to ignoring safety standards. You can't just show me a piece of paper and expect me to unsee a whole year of them actively trying to ruin my reputation. Distrustful? No, no, not at all. I mean, if you look at my track record before all this started, before I really started seeing what they were doing with the safety reports... I was probably the most trusting guy in the depot. \n\nHonestly, back when I was just starting out, right out of high school when I was a junior mechanic, I was the guy who would lend you my personal torque wrench or my diagnostic scanner and not even ask when you were going to give it back. I just took everything at face value. \n\nThat's what makes this whole situation so incredibly frustrating, Doc. I wasn't sitting around looking for people to plot against me.
